work.title: Built, tested, delivered.
work.description: The closest match to this role comes first. Open any card for the full story.
work.libraryTitle: Six more systems, built the same way.

rate-table.title: High-precision Inertial Rate Table
rate-table.hook: A table that turns at a rate you can trust, so a gyroscope can be judged against it.
rate-table.challenge: Deliver steady, programmable rotation across a wide speed range, while keeping the machine easy to service and practical to build.
rate-table.work: Led the mechanism, drivetrain, sensing, control integration, fabrication coordination, and iterative validation. Combined mechanical refinement with encoder feedback and repeatable test routines.
rate-table.result: Client-side analysis measured 32.8 ppmFS encoder-to-command nonlinearity over a ±300 dps sweep. The final client-run session also demonstrated sinusoidal motion up to 15 Hz at 400 dps peak.
rate-table.alt: Custom inertial rate table test equipment

sensory.title: Visual Sensory Learning Product Line
sensory.hook: From a custom device to a repeatable product line.
sensory.challenge: Create a robust, engaging sensory product that could be manufactured repeatedly, maintained easily, and supplied at meaningful volume.
sensory.work: Led product iteration, mechanical/electrical integration, fabrication methods, assembly improvements, test checks, and coordination with the permanent engineering and technician team.
sensory.result: Around 300 cumulative units delivered for one client product line; the client exports units to Gulf and European markets.

chewing.title: Chewing Simulator
chewing.hook: A rig that has to chew for months without drifting.
chewing.challenge: Reproduce chewing motion and load over hundreds of thousands of cycles, in water held at body temperature, without losing alignment or accuracy along the way.
chewing.work: 2040 aluminium extrusion frame for rigidity and modular assembly. The Z-axis runs on a NEMA 23 stepper and ballscrew, guided by linear rods and carrying up to 15 kg per head to apply controlled force on the samples.
chewing.result: The rig ran the thermomechanical ageing for a published dental study: 48 prepared molars across three restorative groups, 250,000 mechanical cycles with 1,000 thermal cycles running simultaneously.

ventilator.title: Emergency Ventilator Prototype
ventilator.hook: A rapid-response prototype developed under urgent constraints.
ventilator.challenge: Translate clinical and airflow needs into a buildable mechanism while managing safety, repeatability, and limited development time.
ventilator.work: Supported mechanical architecture, airflow-path development, CAD, fabrication, control integration, and physical iteration.
ventilator.result: A functional engineering prototype used to explore the design space; not represented as a certified medical device.

insulin.title: Automated Insulin Delivery Research Prototype
insulin.hook: A pump that checks its own dose three different ways.
insulin.challenge: Commercial insulin pumps are expensive, and dosing faults are a documented safety problem. The brief was a compact pump that a patient could actually afford, that verifies every dose it delivers.
insulin.work: Geared actuation driving a power screw, with the delivered volume cross-checked by three independent signals: an encoder on the drive, a potentiometer reading absolute linear position, and a current sensor watching the motor.
insulin.result: 99% dosing accuracy in bench testing, at roughly a 90% cost reduction against commercial pumps. Published at IEEE ITC-Egypt 2025.

arcade.title: Falling Sticks & Buzz Wire for EBank
arcade.hook: Two branded arcade games built to survive a crowd.
arcade.challenge: Build reaction games that pull a crowd in, keep working after hundreds of players in one day, and arrive finished on a fixed event date.
arcade.work: Led the game mechanism, the frame and enclosure fabrication, the sensors and electronics, the game logic and scoring, the branded finish, and the testing before delivery.
arcade.result: Falling Sticks and Buzz Wire delivered to EBank, and run again at public startup events with the MARS-Z branding.
arcade.alt: MARS-Z Falling Sticks arcade game being played at a live event

hourglass.title: Digital LED Hourglass
hourglass.hook: A playful object turned into a complete connected prototype.
hourglass.challenge: Make a physical object that senses how it is tilted, and makes digital light behave like real falling sand.
hourglass.work: Integrated the enclosure, LED matrix, motion sensing, controller, prototype PCB, firmware behavior, and companion-app touchpoint using AI-assisted development where useful.
hourglass.result: A working end-to-end prototype demonstrating mechanical, electronic, embedded, and interface integration.

rov.title: MATE ROV Competition System
rov.hook: A competition robot engineered, tested, and operated as a team.
rov.challenge: Build a controllable underwater robot around buoyancy, propulsion, waterproofing, visibility, and real mission tasks.
rov.work: Contributed to mechanical and systems development, rapid troubleshooting, test operations, and team delivery under competition constraints.
rov.result: First place at the MATE ROV Egypt national competition.

cfd.title: Simulation-led Mechanical Design
cfd.hook: Make the expensive mistakes in simulation first.
cfd.challenge: Understand flow, thermal, stress, and deformation behavior early enough to change the design — not merely document it.
cfd.work: Set up and interpreted ANSYS CFD and FEA studies, checked assumptions and boundary conditions, and fed the results back into CAD and prototype decisions.
cfd.result: Earlier risk discovery, fewer blind prototype iterations, and clearer evidence behind mechanical design decisions.

care.title: MARS-Z Care
care.hook: A bilingual critical-care workflow product tested on Android against a live server.
care.challenge: ICU and PICU teams were relying on fragmented paper records, making handover, attribution, rapid review, and longitudinal patient tracking unnecessarily difficult.
care.work: Led product architecture and AI-assisted development integration across a Flutter application, FastAPI backend, PostgreSQL database, offline workflows, PDF handover, and review-before-save Arabic and English voice capture.
care.result: A working full-stack product tested on Android and connected to a live server. It is not represented as a deployed or clinically approved medical system.
care.alt: MARS-Z Care ICU and PICU Android application

arc.title: Arc-discharge Research Systems
arc.hook: Custom laboratory hardware made repeatable across three systems.
arc.challenge: Package a demanding experimental process into an operable, repeatable, and maintainable university research system.
arc.work: Developed the mechanical enclosure and fixtures, integrated subsystems, coordinated fabrication, and standardized assembly and delivery.
arc.result: Three identical systems delivered to a university client in Oman.

mannequin.title: Animatronic Mannequin
mannequin.hook: A shop mannequin given moving arms and a moving head.
mannequin.challenge: Fit a drive mechanism for both arms and the head inside a slim mannequin body, keep the motion smooth and quiet in a public space, and keep every part reachable for service.
mannequin.work: Designed the shoulder and neck mechanism, the drive train, the laser-cut frame, the motor mounting, the wiring, and the motion control. Built it in the workshop and tuned the travel limits by hand.
mannequin.result: A working animatronic mannequin with driven arm and head motion.
mannequin.alt: Animatronic mannequin shoulder mechanism with stepper drive and lead screw

about.title: I work where everything has to meet.
paragraphs: I am a Mechanical Engineering M.Sc. and Lead R&D / Product Development Engineer at MARS-Z. My best work sits where mechanics, electronics, control, the workshop, suppliers, and users all have to become one working product.

I lead a permanent team of 3 engineers and 4 full-time technicians. I use AI to move faster on software and documentation. My firmware and prototype-PCB work is integration level, not specialist level, and I say that upfront.
about.highlight: I also shoot competitive archery — the same discipline of precision, repeatability, and calm focus carries into my engineering work.

challenge.launchBody: Three real trade-offs from actual projects. Your answers show how you think.

rounds.question: The brief is vague, but the deadline is moving. What do you do first?

options.label: Freeze the CAD and start machining.
options.title: Fast start, expensive finish.
options.feedback: You gained visible speed, but unresolved acceptance criteria usually reappear as rework.

options.label: Define acceptance tests and build a quick risk rig.
options.title: Best systems move.
options.feedback: A small experiment buys clarity before detail design locks the wrong assumptions in.

options.label: Add every sensor you might need.
options.title: More data is not always more certainty.
options.feedback: Instrumentation helps only when each measurement answers a defined engineering question.

rounds.question: The mechanism vibrates near the 15 Hz target. What is your next move?

options.label: Thicken every bracket.
options.title: The safe-looking answer has a mass penalty.
options.feedback: Blanket stiffness can shift the problem, overload the drivetrain, and hide the actual excitation source.

options.label: Measure, isolate the mode, then rebalance and tune.
options.title: Evidence before reinforcement.
options.feedback: Separate structural, imbalance, and control effects so each fix has a reason and a verification test.

options.label: Lower the advertised target frequency.
options.title: The prototype survives; the requirement does not.
options.feedback: Changing a requirement is valid only when the stakeholder accepts the product trade-off.

rounds.question: The prototype works. The client now wants hundreds. What changes first?

options.label: Repeat the one-off build exactly.
options.title: A prototype process is not a production process.
options.feedback: Hidden craftsmanship and undocumented adjustments multiply variation as volume grows.

options.label: Run DFM, add jigs, test points, and an acceptance checklist.
options.title: You turned a build into a product line.
options.feedback: Repeatability comes from designed interfaces, controlled variation, and a test that every unit can pass.

options.label: Send the drawings out and inspect at the end.
options.title: Supplier speed without process visibility.
options.feedback: Late inspection catches failures after value has already been added. Critical characteristics need earlier control.

high.title: Prototype saved — systems thinker.
high.text: You balanced delivery speed with measurable reliability and cost control. That is the product-development loop I use on real hardware.

fast.title: Fast builder, exposed validation.
fast.text: You kept momentum high, but the system carries hidden technical debt. Add earlier tests and isolate the highest-cost failure mode.

default.title: Prototype recovered — one more validation pass.
default.text: The engineering direction is sound. Strengthen the acceptance test and manufacturing feedback loop before calling it delivered.
